title: Great Britain
wiki_lead:
Great Britain is an island in the North Atlantic Ocean off the north-west coast of continental Europe, consisting of the countries England, Scotland and Wales, which comprise most of the United Kingdom. With an area of 209,331 km2 (80,823 sq mi), it is the largest of the British Isles, the largest European island, and the ninth-largest island in the world. It is dominated by a maritime climate with narrow temperature differences between seasons. The island of Ireland, with an area 40 per cent that of Great Britain, is to the west. These islands, along with over 1,000 smaller surrounding islands and named substantial rocks, comprise the British Isles archipelago.
The term "Great Britain" can also refer to the entire political territory of England, Scotland and Wales, including their offshore islands. This territory, together with Northern Ireland, constitutes the United Kingdom.
Connected to mainland Europe until 9,000 years ago by a land bridge now known as Doggerland, the island of Great Britain has been inhabited by modern humans for around 30,000 years. In 2011, it had a population of about 61 million, making it the world's third-most-populous island after Java in Indonesia and Honshu in Japan, and the most populated island outside of Asia.

Terminology


Toponymy

The archipelago has been referred to by a single name for over 2000 years: the term 'British Isles' derives from terms used by classical geographers to describe this island group. By 50 BC, Greek geographers were using equivalents of Prettanikē as a collective name for the British Isles. However, with the Roman conquest of Britain, the Latin term Britannia was used for the island of Great Britain, and later Roman-occupied Britain south of Caledonia.
The earliest known name for Great Britain is Albion (Greek: Ἀλβιών) or insula Albionum, from either the Latin albus meaning "white" (possibly referring to the white cliffs of Dover, the first view of Britain from the continent) or the "island of the Albiones". The oldest mention of terms related to Great Britain was by Aristotle (384–322 BC), or possibly by Pseudo-Aristotle, in his text On the Universe, Vol. III. To quote his works, "There are two very large islands in it, called the British Isles, Albion and Ierne".

The first known written use of the word Britain was an ancient Greek transliteration of the original Proto-Celtic term in a work on the travels and discoveries of Pytheas that has not survived. The earliest existing records of the word are quotations of the periplus by later authors, such as those within Strabo's Geographica, Pliny's Natural History and Diodorus of Sicily's Bibliotheca historica. Pliny the Elder (AD 23–79) in his Natural History records of Great Britain: "Its former name was Albion; but at a later period, all the islands, of which we shall just now briefly make mention, were included under the name of 'Britanniæ.'"
The name Britain descends from the Latin name for Britain, Britannia or Brittānia, the land of the Britons. The French form replaced the Old English Breoton, Breoten, Bryten, Breten (also Breoton-lond, Breten-lond). Britannia was used by the Romans from the 1st century BC for the British Isles taken together. It is derived from the travel writings of Pytheas around 320 BC, which described various islands in the North Atlantic as far north as Thule (probably Norway).
The peoples of these islands of Prettanike were called the Πρεττανοί, Priteni or Pretani. Priteni is the source of the Welsh language term Prydain, Britain, which has the same source as the Goidelic term Cruithne used to refer to the early Brythonic-speaking inhabitants of the Scottish highlands and the north of Scotland. The latter were later called Picts or Caledonians by the Romans. grok_lead: Great Britain, also known as Albion, is the largest island in the British Isles, located off the northwestern coast of continental Europe and separated from the mainland by the North Sea, English Channel, and Atlantic Ocean; it consists of the countries of the United Kingdom: England, Scotland, and Wales. The island covers 209,331 square kilometres and ranks as the ninth-largest island globally, accounting for the bulk of the United Kingdom's land area excluding Northern Ireland. Its population was estimated at 67.6 million as of mid-2025, concentrated in urban centres like London, Birmingham, Manchester, and Glasgow. Geographically diverse, Great Britain features rugged Highlands in Scotland, rolling Pennines in England, and mountainous regions in Wales, with lowland plains supporting intensive agriculture and urbanisation. The island's temperate maritime climate fosters varied ecosystems, from moorlands and forests to coastal wetlands, though intensive land use has reduced native habitats. Historically, human settlement dates back tens of thousands of years, with Celtic Britons inhabiting the region before Roman conquest in 43 AD, followed by Anglo-Saxon migrations, Viking incursions, and Norman invasion in 1066 that shaped medieval feudal structures. From the 16th century, Great Britain emerged as a naval power, establishing the British Empire that by 1922 encompassed a quarter of the Earth's land surface and population, facilitating global trade, migration, and cultural exchange while involving conquest and resource extraction. The 18th and 19th centuries saw the Industrial Revolution originate here, driven by innovations in steam power, textiles, and iron production, propelling economic dominance and urbanisation. Scientific advancements, including foundational work in physics by Isaac Newton and evolutionary theory by Charles Darwin, underscore intellectual contributions that influenced global modernity. In the 20th century, Great Britain played pivotal roles in both World Wars, with the Battle of Britain in 1940 marking a key defensive victory against aerial invasion, and postwar decolonisation reshaping its global stance amid economic shifts and the formation of the welfare state. Today, as the core of the United Kingdom, it maintains a developed economy emphasizing finance, technology, and services, though challenges include regional devolution tensions, post-Brexit trade adjustments, and debates over imperial legacies versus achievements in law, governance, and parliamentary democracy.
